rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Anthropic just handed a piece of your code pipeline to an AI. Not to review it. Not to flag it. To *approve* it and merge it.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's the part that stops me. It's not suggesting anymore. It's deciding.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And they've made the beta free to try, with ten thousand dollars in credits dangled in front of anyone willing to find out what that actually means.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Welcome to The AI Edge. I'm Alex, with Jamie and Rufus. It is Tuesday, November twenty-fourth, twenty twenty-six, and yes — the AI is now the one who signs off on your code. Today: Anthropic's new agent suite, Meta's shopping agent just landed in the UK, and DeepMind says it's using AI to redesign quantum algorithms.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Today’s episode is brought to you by The Ledger. What changed in AI, and what does it mean for your next decision?

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The Ledger turns the noise into five focused briefings. Subscribe at T-H-E-L-E-D-G-R dot I-O. That’s LEDGR, with no E between G and R. Find the link in our show notes.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Okay. Claude Ship. Let's actually explain what this is, because the name does not tell you.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The name sounds like a logistics startup that failed in 2019.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Heh. So — Anthropic released this on November twenty-third. It's a suite of three AI agents built specifically around GitHub pull requests. Code Review is generally available. PR Steward and Claude Approvals are both in beta.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And the distinction between those three matters enormously.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Tell me.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Code Review analyses your code — that's the familiar part, AI as reader. PR Steward goes one step further: it handles merge conflicts, pushes fixes, responds to feedback. But it cannot actually approve a merge.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And that's where Claude Approvals comes in.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Exactly. Claude Approvals is the one that can authorize the merge itself, based on policies that the team defines.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So your team writes the rules, and then the AI becomes the gatekeeper that enforces them without anyone having to click approve.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which sounds reasonable in the abstract, and I want to stay there for a moment, because I think we sprint past that too quickly. The pull request approval — that's the quality gate. That's the last human checkpoint before code goes into the codebase.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Right.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And Anthropic is not saying "here's an AI that helps you do that job." They're saying "here's an AI that *is* that job."

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: They do recommend running it in observe-only mode first. So there's a proposed on-ramp.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Observe-only. Meaning it watches what it would have done, without actually doing it.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Which is either reassuringly cautious or mildly terrifying, depending on how long your team actually runs it that way before someone gets impatient.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That is the question, isn't it. How long does "observe-only" last before a VP says "okay this seems fine, ship it."

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Three weeks if you're lucky.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: One sprint if you're not.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So practically — for a developer listening to this on the way to work — what does the day actually look like if their organization turns this on?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Imagine you're on a team that's been moving fast, writing a lot of AI-generated code, and your review queue is backed up. That's specifically the problem Anthropic is targeting here, by the way — AI-heavy workflows that produce more code than human reviewers can keep pace with.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So the volume problem is real.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Genuinely real. If you're using AI to generate code, you're generating more code than your team was sized to review. So your options are: hire more reviewers, slow down generation, or change what reviewing means.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And this is option three.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: This is option three. Claude Approvals steps into the gap, checks whether the PR meets your team's defined policies, and merges if it does.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: What can go wrong?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Well — the AI applies the policies you gave it. So if your policies are incomplete, or if the edge case wasn't covered, the approval happens anyway.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And this is worth flagging: Anthropic's own guidance says organizations using HIPAA-configured environments or customer-managed encryption keys cannot use this. That's a real exclusion for a lot of enterprise healthcare and financial-services teams.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So it's not for every enterprise yet.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Not by a long way.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: There's a credits offer attached to this, which I think is interesting.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Eligible enterprise organizations can claim ten thousand dollars in credits by January fifteenth, twenty twenty-seven. Which is a meaningful number for a beta product — it lowers the experimentation cost and effectively says "try it before you decide."

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: It's also a way to get usage data from real production environments without having to build a formal pilot program.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's a bit cynical.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I didn't say it was bad. It's how software betas work. You're trading access for signal.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The more interesting question to me is what this reveals about where Anthropic thinks the value is. They've moved from "Claude helps you write code" to "Claude governs whether code ships."

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's a meaningful shift in authority.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: It's the shift from the AI being a junior developer to being — not quite a senior developer, but something like a CI/CD policy that can read intent, not just syntax.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: CI/CD, for anyone not neck-deep in this — that's continuous integration and continuous deployment. It's the automated pipeline that takes code from "written" to "running in production." Approvals are historically the human checkpoints inside that pipeline.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And Claude Approvals is now one of those checkpoints. So what do you actually do if your team is considering this?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Honestly? Audit your existing policies first. Before you hand approval authority to any system — human or AI — you need to know what your policies actually say. Because if they're vague, the AI will make a judgment call. It just won't tell you it made one.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's the useful bit. The AI will not surface its own uncertainty the way a nervous junior dev might ping you at ten p.m. saying "I wasn't sure about this one."

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Right. It approved it. Done. You find out later.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Which means the audit of "what do our policies actually cover" is not optional pre-work. It's the whole job.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Okay. What changed: AI agents can now hold approval authority in a software pipeline, not just advisory positions. Who benefits first: fast-moving dev teams with high AI-generated code volume, if they invest the time upfront to define rigorous policies. Who should wait: anyone in HIPAA environments — or any team that hasn't yet formalized what "good enough to merge" actually means.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Our second story — Meta launched something in the UK yesterday that I genuinely think is worth pausing on. It is not vaporware. It is in people's phones.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Muse.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Muse. Meta's personal AI agent, live as of November twenty-third for UK users eighteen and older. iOS, Android, WhatsApp, the web. And it can book you a train, order your Ocado shop, do things at Marks and Spencer.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Just absorb that for a second. This is not "AI suggests recipes." This is "AI buys your groceries."

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: With one important condition. Every transaction requires your explicit approval through a secure credentials store.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: So it cannot spend your money without asking.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: At least by design.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That qualifier is doing a lot of work in a very small space.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: It is. And I want to explain why, because it matters. The acknowledged open problem here is prompt injection — which sounds technical but isn't a complicated idea. Someone buries text in a product listing that looks like an instruction to the agent. Muse reads the page, reads the hidden command — and follows it instead of yours. Meta has listed this as a known issue. The purchase-approval step is the main practical guard against it.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: So someone could theoretically put something in a grocery listing that tells Muse to do something you never asked for.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Theoretically, yes. No specific mitigation has been published. The approval step is what's standing between you and that.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Rufus, take us on location.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Right. Picture the digital checkout queue at Ocado — Britain's grocery delivery platform, entirely software-defined, no physical stores, everything lives in an app. Muse, as of yesterday, can operate inside that environment on your behalf. It browses, builds a basket, presents it to you, and when you approve, it completes the purchase. What's architecturally interesting is that Muse isn't a tab inside Ocado's app. You bring Muse to the retailer. The agent is the interface.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which tells you something about where the confidence in this model is coming from.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: It does. And it has a sharp implication for anyone not currently integrated with Muse. The customer may never visit your website the way they used to.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Back to the wider story. So what happens to retailers who aren't in the system yet?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Good if you're indexed and showing up in results. Potentially quite bad if you're not. The parallel to search isn't subtle — you either appear or you don't exist.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Right now Ocado, M&S, and Trainline are in. Everyone else is watching.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Which loops back to the question I actually want answered. If you have to approve every single transaction, is the agent actually saving you time? Or have they built a very polished extra step?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I've been thinking about this. It depends entirely on what Muse does before the approval. If it's already found the cheapest return train to Edinburgh, checked three departure times, cross-referenced your calendar, and is now presenting you with one button — the approval takes three seconds. That's not a limitation. That's a finish line.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: But if it's presenting you the same list you'd have found yourself in four clicks, the approval step is friction with branding on it.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Yes. And that is the thing we genuinely cannot answer yet, because this launched yesterday. We're working from what Meta described, not from three weeks of people actually using it.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So the value is entirely in what happens upstream of the confirmation.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Exactly. The curation, the comparison, the decision. If that's good, the approval is painless. If that's mediocre, the approval is annoying and you just go back to doing it yourself.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And the retailer question is live right now. Ocado, M&S, Trainline are indexed. Everyone else is making a decision about whether to be.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: A short sponsor break for The Ledger. Alex, if everything is breaking news, when are we supposed to get any work done?

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's the question The Ledger helps you work through: five focused briefings connecting AI news with the decisions in front of you.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The Ledger. Because reading another headline is a marvellous way to postpone deciding anything. I admire the efficiency of the procrastination.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Rufus has diagnosed the problem. The Ledger link is in our show notes. Back to the story.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Our third story is different in texture from the other two. No product you can download. No beta you can sign up for.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which might actually make it the most consequential of the three.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: That's a bold pre-empt.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Let me earn it.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Google DeepMind published a research post on November twenty-third describing work where teams of Gemini 4 agents worked on quantum algorithms. The result, DeepMind says, is highly efficient quantum circuits with potential applications in fusion energy, chemistry, and enzyme simulation.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Quantum circuits — for anyone not spending their lunch break with physics papers—

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which is definitely all of us.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: —a quantum circuit is essentially the instruction set for a quantum computer. You want it to solve a specific problem, you hand it a sequence of operations designed for that problem. Designing efficient ones for genuinely hard problems is itself a genuinely hard problem.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And that design challenge is what the agents worked on.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Right. This isn't "AI uses a quantum computer." It's "AI helps design better programs for quantum computers." Different thing entirely.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: What's the formal verification piece?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: DeepMind links to something called the Lean framework. Lean is a proof-checking system used in mathematics — it doesn't just test whether a proof seems right, it verifies that it actually is. So the improved algorithms weren't just run and observed, they were checked analytically.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Which matters. In quantum computing, empirical testing is expensive and noisy. Formal verification catches errors before you ever run the hardware.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So what are the actual applications they name?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Fusion energy — simulations of plasma behavior. Chemistry — molecular simulations for drug discovery or materials science. Enzymes — which connects to pharmaceutical biology. Three different fields where simulation is currently the bottleneck.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Because the physical experiment is too slow or too expensive.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Or physically impossible at scale. You simulate instead. Better quantum algorithms mean more accurate, more efficient simulations.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And DeepMind is careful. They say the work "could one day" support these applications. They are not claiming they've solved fusion.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Worth holding onto, that qualifier.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Very much so. The specific thing that happened is: agents using formal verification improved known quantum algorithms. That's a real, measurable advance in method. What happens downstream in actual deployed science is still prospective.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: If the method is repeatable — and that's genuinely the open question — then it's not just about quantum algorithms. It's about whether formal verification plus agent collaboration works as a general approach to hard mathematical problems.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: DeepMind is implicitly positioning it that way. The paper's there if you want to check the specifics. But we're working from the research post, not a peer-review response.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Fairly standard for a forty-eight-hour window.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Who does this actually affect right now?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Researchers, primarily. If you're in quantum computing, you have a potentially faster path to algorithm improvement with formal verification as the quality gate. That's immediately interesting to the field.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And for people in fusion or chemistry — this is worth watching not because the tool is in your hands today, but because the timeline on quantum advantage for real problems may have moved. We don't know by how much.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's the honest version. Progress happened. The timeline question is still open, and it won't close until other labs try the same approach.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Try me.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Picture explaining this to someone over dinner. AI didn't use a quantum computer. AI designed a better program for a quantum computer. Formally verified. And the target applications include plasma fusion and drug discovery. Someone will say "so the robots are doing physics homework now?" And the answer is — kind of, yes —

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: and the homework got a perfect score.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I mean. That is what happened.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Alright. Jamie's been testing something this week and I think today is the day.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Oh good. I do love being the demonstration case.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: You volunteered. I have the message.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I did volunteer. So. We've been talking about agents that review code and agents that handle procurement, and I wanted to test something more unglamorous. I work with a lot of dense documents — research posts, long PDFs, papers with qualifications buried in the fourth paragraph.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The comprehension gap.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Exactly that. The gap between reading something and actually knowing how to use it. I can get through a DeepMind research post in four minutes. Figuring out whether the Lean framework result is as significant as the framing suggests — that takes real time.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: So you handed it to an agent.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I did. I asked it to identify the specific technical claim, isolate the qualifications, and flag where the post's framing might be running ahead of the evidence.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Genuinely useful. It caught the "could one day" language immediately — exactly the soft future-tense that disappears in a fast read. It also cross-referenced the Lean mention with what Lean actually does, which I'd have had to look up separately anyway.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: So it's doing the footnote work in real time.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Yes. The limitation is it doesn't know what I already know. It flagged things I didn't need flagged, and I had to filter. The signal-to-noise ratio depends entirely on how precisely you've described your actual knowledge gap at the start.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So the prompt is still the skill.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The prompt is still the skill. Tell it you're a PhD chemist who doesn't need the quantum circuit primer, and it adjusts. If you don't tell it, you get the primer.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: But if you do specify—

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Then it's fast and quite precise. Forty-minute careful read became a ten-minute review. That's real time back, consistently.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I want to find fault with this and I cannot.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: There's the warmth. Precisely rationed as always.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Don't push it.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Jamie, show us the AI transformation.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Here is a detail that caught me properly off guard. A small bakery owner, staring at a city festival announcement on their phone, now has a system that already knows what that event means for their flour order.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: That is either impressive or slightly unsettling.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Maybe both. But let me back up, because the before state here is genuinely relatable if you have ever run any kind of small food business.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Or ordered too much of anything based on a feeling.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which is most of us. So the problem SAP documented at TechEd 2026, announced in November of that year, is called the bullwhip effect. Independent bakeries and small food manufacturers tend to over-order ingredients when they sense demand is rising, and under-order when things feel slow. The result is either a walk-in full of flour going stale or a sudden stockout the weekend a local race happens to end near the shop.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Ordering by vibes, essentially.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Ordering by vibes. And the cost of vibes, in perishable goods, is spoilage or empty shelves. Neither is a great business outcome.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So what does the agent actually do?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The bakery connects two things it probably already has: historical sales records and a local event calendar. Those feed into a workflow built on SAP Integrated Business Planning, which SAP calls IBP, with embedded AI agents handling what SAP describes as agentic orchestration. The agent monitors incoming orders alongside that external calendar data continuously.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: So when a city festival shows up on the calendar—

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The agent finds the correlation to what sales looked like during prior comparable events, updates its demand forecast, and drafts a revised replenishment order. It does not place the order. It flags the draft for the owner.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That handoff moment is the part I want to understand better.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: It is the part worth dwelling on. The owner opens the flagged draft, sees the AI-adjusted projection, and can compare it against current cash flow before deciding anything. They hit confirm to execute, or they do not. The agent has done the data work. The human makes the financial commitment.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: So the agent reads the calendar so the owner does not have to do the mental arithmetic at eleven at night.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That is a reasonable way to put it. And the human review is not a formality. It is structurally necessary, which SAP's own documentation makes clear.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: I want to pick at the limitation here, because a festival is a tidy example. What about something messier?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That is precisely where it breaks down, and SAP says so explicitly. The agent cannot anticipate what SAP calls black swan events. A sudden local closure, a supplier disruption, something with no historical pattern to draw from. In those cases the agent's suggestion could be confidently wrong, and human oversight is what catches that.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The limitation is not a footnote. It is built into how the system is meant to operate.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Confidently wrong with perishable inventory is a costly combination.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which is why the confirm step is not optional elegance. It is the actual safeguard.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Now, I have to ask, because this is a SAP TechEd announcement case drawing on pilot SME customers. What is the evidence quality here?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Fair challenge and I want to be direct about it. The result basis is SAP TechEd 2026 documentation. SAP reports qualitative improvement in inventory turnover and reduced spoilage among pilot small and medium enterprise customers. Those are SAP's characterizations of their own pilot. This is a single major attributed source. It is not an independent audit and I am not presenting it as one. The improvement is real enough for SAP to document it. What we do not have is a neutral third-party measurement.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: So we believe it is probably working but we are not waving a verified percentage.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: We are not waving a verified percentage. The directional finding, that event-aware replenishment outperforms gut-check ordering for perishables, is intuitively sound. The specific magnitude is what requires the source caveat.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Right. Speaking of intuition, Rufus, when did you last order something based on a feeling and regret it?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I ordered three kilograms of specialty coffee on the assumption a dinner party was imminent. The dinner party has not materialized.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: You need this workflow more than the bakery does.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I need a local event calendar and lower confidence in my own social life.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The agent would have flagged that order for review and you would have reconsidered.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The agent would have been right and I would have ignored it. That is also a known human behavior.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And that is actually the honest version of the limitation. The human in the loop can override the agent for bad reasons as well as good ones. The system works when the owner genuinely uses the review step as a check, not as a rubber stamp.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: What does the transition from manual ordering actually look like in practice, though? Because connecting SAP IBP to a local event calendar sounds like it requires some technical lift for a small bakery.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: It requires setup, yes. SAP IBP is available within the cloud update for smaller enterprise tiers, so it is not locked behind the largest licensing tiers, but it is still enterprise software. A bakery owner is not installing this themselves on a Sunday afternoon. The honest first step for someone listening who recognizes their own inventory gut-check process in this story is to audit it before looking at any tool. Count how many times in the last quarter you ordered based on anticipated demand rather than observed orders.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: If the answer is frequently and you have spoilage records to match, you have a concrete problem. Then look for tools that allow external calendar data to feed into replenishment workflows. SAP IBP is one option at this availability tier. The principle applies more broadly.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: So the first step is not downloading anything. It is counting your spoiled flour.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: It is counting your spoiled flour. That number is the honest brief for whatever comes next.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And the reason this changes how the business works, not just one order, is what exactly?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The shift is from reactive to anticipatory. Manual ordering responds to what already happened. Event-aware replenishment responds to what the data suggests is coming. For perishables, that timing difference is the whole business. You cannot unspoil a croissant.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: That may be the most useful sentence ever spoken in this segment.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I will take it. The case is from SAP TechEd 2026, the pilot findings are SAP's own reported outcomes, and the tool is generally available in SAP IBP's smaller enterprise cloud tier. The agent does the calendar reading. The owner does the confirming. That division is what makes it actually useful rather than just automatic.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's Jamie's AI transformation.

sound_design.edit: approved source: shortened tail and fade only

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Okay. The title question: what is Claude Ship actually changing?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The authority structure inside a software team. Not just what AI can do — who AI can be.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Before yesterday, the AI was an advisor. Now, with Claude Approvals, it's a decision-maker with defined scope.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And that scope matters enormously. Because the policies you define are the ceiling of safety in this system. Anthropic says run it in observe-only first. The teams that do that carefully will get different results than the teams that give it three days and move on.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: There's a checkable prediction here: in six months, we will start seeing reports from teams about what their observe-only period revealed — either "this would have caught more than we expected" or "this would have approved things we'd have blocked." Those reports will tell you whether the beta warning is real caution or just liability language.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That is the thing to watch. And the thing to do if your team is considering this: before you define the policies, map the gaps. Find the edge cases your current human reviewers handle with judgment rather than a written rule, because those are exactly the cases the AI will either miss or flatten.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Muse in the UK is the other thing to watch. The approval-per-transaction model is Meta's answer to the security question they admit they haven't solved. Whether that feels like safety or friction will determine whether this scales.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And DeepMind's quantum result — the method is the story. Agent-assisted formal verification as a repeatable scientific workflow. Watch whether other labs try to replicate it.
